1233.title: The boy who knew everything but this
1233.hook: Shvetaketu comes home after twelve years of study, proud, and his father asks the one question he can't answer
1233.carry: you are that: the self is never lost, only unseen
1233.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, students hear the Upanishads' great sayings, such as you are that, from a teacher, reflect on them, and sit with the question of what the self is; Shankara's commentary on the first sutra is a classic place to begin.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and Shankara's preface: the I and the this, mixed up like silver seen on a shell.

In the Chandogya Upanishad, a boy named Shvetaketu leaves home at twelve to study the Vedas. He comes back at twenty-four, having learned them all, and he walks in proud, sure he knows everything. His father, Uddalaka, asks him one question. Did you ask for the teaching by which what hasn't been heard becomes heard, what hasn't been thought becomes thought, what isn't known becomes known? Shvetaketu has no idea what he means. So his father gives a clue: know one lump of clay, and you know everything made of clay; the pots are only names. Shvetaketu admits it. My teachers can't have known this, or they'd have told me. Please, sir, teach me. And lesson after lesson, his father ends on the same three words, usually rendered: you are that.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS OF STUDY.` → `ONE QUESTION HE CAN'T ANSWER.` → `YOU ARE THAT.`

segments.voice: Centuries later, Shankara opens his commentary on the Brahma Sutra with Shvetaketu's problem. The first line says: now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman. But is Brahman known already, or not? If known, why inquire? If wholly unknown, how could anyone even want it? His answer: Brahman is known, in a way, because it is the self of everyone. Nobody ever thinks, I am not. What's in doubt is what this self is. Some say the body, some the senses, some the mind, some a flicker of awareness, some a self that acts and enjoys. Shvetaketu was just like that: full of learning, unclear about the one thing closest to him. Shankara's own answer is the father's: the self, atman, is Brahman, the reality behind everything. That is the heart of Advaita Vedanta. So jnana isn't finding a new object. It's clarity about what was never missing. Other Vedanta schools honor the same three words and read them differently; Ramanuja, for one, hears in them the Lord as the inner self of every self. Today, plenty of people travel far to find themselves. This teaching turns the search around: the one looking is what's being looked for.
screen: `KNOWN, OR UNKNOWN?` · `NOBODY THINKS: I AM NOT.` · `ATMAN IS BRAHMAN.` · `THE ONE LOOKING IS THE ONE LOOKED FOR.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and ask, quietly, the question many Advaita teachers give, made famous by Ramana Maharshi: who am I? Let the mind offer its answers, this body, these feelings, these thoughts, and let each one pass without deciding. Come back each time to the plain sense of being here, before any label. If you pray, offer that plain presence; if you don't, simply rest in it.
Jnana. Knowing. On Shankara's reading of the first line, not finding something new, but becoming clear about a self that is never lacking.
Your line: you are that: the self is never lost, only unseen. Shvetaketu knew everything but this. I'll be here tomorrow.

1234.title: Salt in the water
1234.hook: Uddalaka has his son drop salt in water overnight. by morning it's invisible, and still in every sip
1234.carry: jnana is seeing what is, not choosing a belief
1234.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, study of the Upanishads with a teacher is followed by reflection and meditation, so that what is heard becomes direct understanding.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and Shvetaketu: nobody thinks I am not, and you are that.

Shvetaketu still doesn't get it. So his father, Uddalaka, tries something simple. Put this salt in water, he says, and come back in the morning. Next day: bring me the salt. Shvetaketu looks. He can't find it; it has dissolved. Take a sip from the top, his father says. How is it? Salty. From the middle? Salty. From the bottom? Salty. So it was there all along. You don't see it, Uddalaka says, but it is here. In the same way, the finest essence, the self of this whole world, is here, though you don't see it. That is the real. That is the self. And you are that, Shvetaketu.
screen: `SALT IN THE WATER.` → `GONE FROM SIGHT.` → `SALTY IN EVERY SIP.`

segments.voice: Notice what happens: Shvetaketu doesn't decide the water is salty. The taste decides. Shankara makes the same point on the Brahma Sutra's second line, which says Brahman is that from which this world is born, held and dissolved. Couldn't you just reason your way to a cause? Not on its own, he says; the line gathers the Upanishads' teachings, and reasoning is welcome as their helper, because the senses can't show Brahman. Then his famous contrast. With action you have choices: do a ritual, skip it, do it another way. Knowing isn't like that. A tall shape glimpsed in poor light may be a post or a man; you can think either, but only one thought is knowledge. Knowing depends on the thing, not on anyone's choosing. Brahman is something that already is, so knowing it isn't picking a belief, and, he says, it's meant to end in direct experience, anubhava, like the taste of salt. That's the Hindu path of jnana: not opinion, but seeing what is. Ramanuja and others join this knowing to loving meditation; Shankara draws his line firmly here. Today faith is often called a personal preference. This tradition says the deepest truth isn't up for choosing; it waits to be tasted.
screen: `THE TASTE DECIDES.` · `DOING HAS CHOICES.` · `KNOWING DEPENDS ON THE THING.` · `MEANT TO END IN EXPERIENCE.`

segments.voice: Take a sip of water, or simply notice your breath. Say silently the words Uddalaka spoke: you are that. Don't argue with them or try to believe them hard; let them sit, the way salt sits in water, and come back to them whenever the mind wanders. Vedanta teachers call this manana, turning over what you've heard. If you pray, let this quiet attention be your prayer; if you don't, simply rest in it.
Jnana. Knowing. For Shankara, knowing that depends on the thing itself, not on anyone's choosing, and that is meant to end in direct experience.
Your line: jnana is seeing what is, not choosing a belief. The salt was in every sip. Go gently.

1235.title: Maitreyi asks for more
1235.hook: Yajnavalkya is about to leave home and offers his wife Maitreyi a share of his wealth. she asks for something else
1235.carry: scripture: breathed out by brahman, and the way to know
1235.howItsDone: Vedanta schools treat the Upanishads as the means of knowing Brahman; in Advaita, students hear them from a teacher (shravana), reflect on them (manana) and meditate on them (nididhyasana).

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and the salt in every sip: knowing depends on what is, not on choosing.

In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, the great sage Yajnavalkya decides to leave home for the wandering life. He tells his wife Maitreyi he'll settle his property between her and his other wife, Katyayani. Maitreyi asks: if this whole earth, full of wealth, were mine, would it make me immortal? No, he says. You'd live like the rich, but there's no hope of immortality through wealth. Then what would I do with it? she answers. Tell me what you know. So he does. The self, he tells her, is what must be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated on. And he says where the Vedas themselves come from: like smoke billowing from a fire of damp wood, they are the breathing out of a great being.
screen: `A SHARE OF THE WEALTH.` → `WOULD IT MAKE ME IMMORTAL?` → `TELL ME WHAT YOU KNOW.`

segments.voice: Shankara leans on that breath when he reads the Brahma Sutra's third line, which says, in effect: because of being the source of scripture. The key word is yoni, a source, a womb. He reads it two ways and keeps both. First: Brahman is the source of scripture. Texts that light up all things like a lamp, he says, can only come from something all-knowing, as easily as breathing. Second: scripture is the source, meaning the way, of knowing Brahman. The senses can't reach it, and reasoning alone can't settle it; the Upanishads can. That's why Hindus call the Veda shruti, what was heard: many hold that no human composed it, and that the seers heard it. And it's why the Advaita path of jnana follows Yajnavalkya's words to Maitreyi: hear the teaching from a teacher, reflect on it, meditate until it's known. Other Vedanta schools comment on this line in their own ways. Today we're surrounded by words, endless feeds of them. This tradition holds that a few words, heard well, can open onto what no screen can show.
screen: `YONI: A SOURCE, A WOMB.` · `SOURCE OF SCRIPTURE, AND THE WAY.` · `SHRUTI: WHAT THE SEERS HEARD.` · `HEAR, REFLECT, MEDITATE.`

1236.title: Nachiketa turns down the horses
1236.hook: Death offers a boy horses, gold and a long life if he'll drop one question. he says keep them
1236.carry: moksha isn't earned; it's what the self already is
1236.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, good action and devotion are often understood as preparing the mind, while freedom itself is understood as coming through knowledge of the self.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and Maitreyi: scripture breathed out by a great being, and the way to know Brahman.

In the Katha Upanishad, a boy named Nachiketa watches his father give away old, worn-out cows at a great sacrifice. To whom will you give me? the boy asks, again and again, until his father snaps: to Death. So Nachiketa goes to the house of Yama, Death himself, and waits three nights without food. Yama, who has left a guest unfed, offers him three wishes. The third: when a person dies, some say they still are, some say they aren't. Teach me. Yama tries to change the subject. Take sons and grandsons who live a hundred years, cattle, elephants, gold, horses, wide lands, as long a life as you like. Nachiketa says: these last only until tomorrow. Keep your horses; keep your songs. And Yama, pleased, praises him: the good and the pleasant come to everyone; the wise choose the good, and you have.
screen: `A BOY AT DEATH'S DOOR.` → `HORSES, GOLD, A LONG LIFE.` → `KEEP THEM.`

segments.voice: Shankara makes the same point in his comment on the Brahma Sutra's fourth line, which says, in effect: but that, because the texts are connected in it. The small word but, he says, turns away an objection from the Mimamsa school, thinkers who take the Veda very seriously and hold that its sentences exist to tell people what to do. So, they say, the Upanishads must be about action too. Shankara answers: no, they teach Brahman, something that already is. His reason echoes Nachiketa. Anything produced by action has a beginning, and whatever begins also ends. If freedom, moksha, were made by action, it would end too. So moksha isn't produced, reached, changed or cleaned up. It's what the self already is, and knowing removes what hid it, the way a lamp shows a room it didn't build. Shankara isn't saying action is pointless; good action and devotion ready the mind. But the last step isn't a doing. Some other Vedanta schools see freedom as the Lord's gift to devotion. Today it's easy to treat even the spiritual life like a points system. Nachiketa waved the prizes away; this teaching says the deepest freedom was never a prize.
screen: `BUT: AN OBJECTION TURNED AWAY.` · `WHAT BEGINS ALSO ENDS.` · `MOKSHA IS NOT MADE.` · `FREEDOM WAS NEVER A PRIZE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind two or three things you'll do today. As each one comes up, offer it in your heart without asking what it will earn; many Hindus do this with a short prayer, or at the family altar in the morning. Then, for a few breaths, stop adding effort, and notice what's already here without making anything. If you don't pray, simply let the reward go.
Jnana. Knowing. On the fourth line, Shankara says freedom isn't produced by any action, so what frees is knowing what already is.

1237.title: The king who stayed king
1237.hook: a king hears the sage Yajnavalkya say the knower's body lies like a snake's old skin. then he goes on ruling
1237.carry: jivanmukti: free while still living in the body
1237.howItsDone: Advaita Vedanta teachers often read the Brahma Sutra's first four lines with students as a summary of the whole work, and hold up sages like King Janaka as pictures of freedom while still living.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and Nachiketa: moksha isn't earned; it's what the self already is.

King Janaka of Videha loves hard questions, and his court is famous for them. When the sage Yajnavalkya visits, the king keeps him talking, about dreams, about deep sleep, about what happens at death, and again and again he says: I'll give you a thousand cows, sir; teach me more, for freedom. So Yajnavalkya describes the one who has let go of every desire in the heart. Such a person, he says, reaches Brahman here, in this life. And he gives a picture. As a snake's cast-off skin lies on an anthill, dead and thrown away, so lies this body. The shape is still there; the snake has moved on. Janaka didn't leave his throne. Hindus remember him as the king who knew the self and kept ruling; the Bhagavad Gita names him among those who reached perfection through action.
screen: `A KING WHO LOVES QUESTIONS.` → `A THOUSAND COWS: TEACH ME MORE.` → `A SKIN ON AN ANTHILL.`

segments.voice: Shankara reaches for this skin near the end of his comment on the Brahma Sutra's fourth line, the last of the four lines we've followed this week. One, the wish to know Brahman. Two, that from which this world comes. Three, the source of scripture. Four, the texts all connect in it. Then the image. Being embodied, Shankara says, comes from the old mix-up, the I taken for the body. When knowing removes the mix-up, the body doesn't vanish. It goes on walking, eating, getting tired. But it's no longer taken for the self. Like the skin on the anthill, it keeps its shape, and nobody is trapped inside it. Advaita teachers call this jivanmukti, freedom while still living. And Shankara adds a test that's hard to forget: someone who has truly understood doesn't live in the turning world the way they did before; someone who still does hasn't understood yet. Many seekers renounce everything, as Shankara himself did; for many Hindus, Janaka shows the knowing doesn't need a cave. Today we're told to find ourselves in our roles: the job, the grades, the image. This teaching says you can carry every role and be held by none.
screen: `A WISH, A POINTER, A SOURCE, A HARMONY.` · `THE BODY NO LONGER TAKEN FOR THE SELF.` · `JIVANMUKTI: FREE WHILE LIVING.` · `EVERY ROLE, HELD BY NONE.`

segments.voice: Feel the whole body sitting, from the soles of the feet to the top of the head, and let the chair or the floor carry its weight. Then name, quietly, the roles you'll carry today: student, child, friend, worker. Hold each one lightly, like a skin with nobody trapped inside. If you pray, offer the day's roles; if you don't, simply rest.
Jnana. Knowing. For Shankara, the knowing that removes the mix-up and changes where you stand, as a snake leaves its skin behind.
Your line: jivanmukti: free while still living in the body. Janaka kept his throne. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1238.title: Indra goes back four times
1238.hook: Indra studies with Prajapati for a hundred and one years, and goes back four times, before he learns what the self is
1238.carry: om: waking, dream, deep sleep, and the self beneath
1238.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta the Mandukya Upanishad is traditionally studied together with Gaudapada's karika and Shankara's commentary, and Om is often chanted at the start and end of Hindu prayer and study.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed a week of jnana with King Janaka: free while still living, the body like a snake's old skin.

In the Chandogya Upanishad, the creator Prajapati announces: there is a self free from old age, death, grief, hunger and thirst. Find it, and you gain every world. Indra, king of the gods, and Virochana, king of the demons, both come to learn, fuel in hand, as students do. After thirty-two years, Prajapati has them look at themselves, dressed in their finest, in a pan of water. Virochana leaves satisfied: the body is the self. Indra, on the road, worries: if the body is blind, is the self blind? Back he goes. Thirty-two more years: the self is the one who roams in dreams. But dreamers weep and are chased. Back again: the self is the one in dreamless sleep. But there he knows nothing at all. Back a fourth time. Now Prajapati says: this body is mortal, the dwelling of a self that is deathless and bodiless.
screen: `A SELF BEYOND DEATH AND GRIEF.` → `A REFLECTION. A DREAMER. A SLEEPER.` → `THE FOURTH TIME.`

segments.voice: Indra climbed through three answers, body, dreamer, deep sleeper, before the fourth. A very short Upanishad, the Mandukya, first met back in year one, maps the same ground, and many teachers read the two side by side. It opens: all this is Om. The self has four quarters. Waking, turned outward to a world of solid things. Dreaming, turned inward to a world made of mind. Deep sleep, where nothing is wanted and no dream is seen, full of ease. And turiya, the fourth, described by what it is not: not inward, not outward, not knowing, not unknowing. Peaceful, not two. That is the self. Then it lays Om over the map: A is waking, U is dreaming, M is deep sleep, and the fourth has no letter; some readers hear it in the silence after. Gaudapada's karika, verses tradition credits to the teacher of Shankara's teacher, says the one self is known as three in the three states. Teachers give this as one reason Om opens and closes so much Hindu prayer: its sounds hold every state a person passes through, and its silence points to the self beneath them.
screen: `ALL THIS IS OM.` · `WAKING, DREAM, SLEEP, AND THE FOURTH.` · `A, U, M, AND THE SILENCE.` · `ONE SELF BENEATH THE THREE.`

segments.voice: If you like, say Om once, softly or silently, and let the sound fade on its own; then rest in the quiet that follows, without filling it. When the mind starts talking, say Om again and rest once more in the quiet after it. If saying Om isn't part of your life, just listen to the room, and to the quiet between sounds; if you pray, let the silence be your prayer.
The Mandukya Karika. Verses, tradition says by Gaudapada, on the Mandukya Upanishad: Om, the three states of waking, dream and deep sleep, and the fourth.

1239.title: Move aside, said Shankara
1239.hook: in Kashi, Shankara tells a man with four dogs to get out of his way. the man asks: move what?
1239.carry: one self, mistaken for many, like rope for snake
1239.howItsDone: Advaita Vedanta teachers use the rope and the snake to explain how the one reality can be taken for something it isn't, and students of Advaita still study the Manisha Panchakam, traditionally credited to Shankara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mandukya Karika and Indra's four trips: om holds waking, dream and deep sleep, and the self beneath.
screen: `OM: THREE SOUNDS AND A SILENCE.` · `A WEEK TO LOOK BACK ON.`

segments.voice: A story told about Shankara. The young teacher has bathed in the Ganges at Kashi and is walking to the temple with his students. Down the narrow lane comes a man the society of the day treated as an outcaste, with four dogs. Move aside, Shankara says. Get out of the way. The man doesn't move. Instead he asks: move what, sir? This body, made of food, away from that body, also made of food? Or the awareness in me away from the awareness in you? Is the sun reflected in the Ganges different from the sun reflected in a puddle in my lane? Shankara stops. Then he bows. The five verses said to come from that moment, the Manisha Panchakam, end the same way each time: whoever sees the one self in all, outcaste or priest, is my teacher. In many tellings, the man was Shiva himself.
screen: `A LANE IN KASHI.` → `MOVE ASIDE.` → `MOVE WHAT, SIR?`

segments.voice: The man's question echoes a teacher before Shankara. Tradition places Gaudapada, author of the Mandukya Karika, as the teacher of Shankara's teacher, and Gaudapada gave Advaita one of its best-known pictures. A rope, not seen clearly in the dark, is imagined as a snake, or a line of water, or other things. When the rope is seen for what it is, the imagining stops. In the same way, he says, the one self is imagined as all kinds of things; when the self is known, the imagining ends. Notice what he doesn't say. The snake didn't turn into the rope or crawl away; it was never anything apart from the rope. That's this week in one picture: Shankara's jnana, the knowing that undoes a mix-up, and Gaudapada's rope. Advaita doesn't say the world is nothing. It says the world is the one reality, seen wrongly; teachers call this maya. That's why the man in the lane could stop Shankara cold: the line between them was the snake. Other schools of Vedanta hold the world real, the Lord's own work. Today we sort people into us and them in a heartbeat. This teaching asks: which of us, exactly, should move?
screen: `THE ROPE TAKEN FOR A SNAKE.` · `THE SNAKE WAS NEVER APART FROM IT.` · `NOT NOTHING: SEEN WRONGLY.` · `WHICH OF US SHOULD MOVE?`

segments.voice: Picture three people you'll see today: someone you love, someone you hardly notice, and someone who irritates you. One at a time, hold each in mind and say silently: the same self. If you like, let your palms meet for each, the way many Hindus greet one another. If you pray, look for the one you pray to in each face; if you don't, simply notice what shifts.
The Mandukya Karika. Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, where a rope seen in the dark as a snake stands for the self taken for all kinds of things.
